job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Gareth Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior accountant at Okoro & Bell, a small tax practice above a dentist's in Birmingham. There are nine of us. I do self-assessment returns for sole traders and landlords, which means a lot of phone calls chasing receipts, then typing figures into the software. I rent a room in a house with two lads from my football team.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's the grind?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that people actually thank you, like the plumber who got a rebate and brought in biscuits. The grind is January, when everyone's returns land at once and I'm in until nine. Mr Bell, who owns the practice, trusts me with the simple ones now. My parents helped me clear my student costs, so I've no debt and a decent bit saved, which is a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. I always thought it was overhyped, like most things in the news. I'd tell the lads it's a gadget for people who want to look clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing much for me, which is how I like it. Okoro & Bell does tax for small people, and that has to be right every time, so Mr Bell is cautious. Still, I'd be nervous that the bigger chains with their software would pinch our customers over time. Birmingham has loads of accounting jobs, so I'd be fine if it went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the returns by hand and finish my ACA exams, which are three a year. I'd keep saving about £500 a month, and I'd probably look at buying a small flat with my girlfriend Tia in a couple of years. Nothing dramatic, I'd just carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. There's a small knot in my stomach about the chains, but it's not a big deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools. Is there a reason?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just don't see what it gives me. I'm slow with new software anyway, it took me three weeks to learn the practice system. I'd rather do a return properly than check what a chatbot did, because I'm the one signing it off. Call it stubborn, but I've seen what happens when a figure is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to stay the same in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The customers, mostly. Our clients are mostly older sole traders who like talking to a person. If those people stay with us, I'm safe. If the big chains start sending cheap packages to the same people, Mr Bell will notice, and we'd be shrinking.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, because it was always overhyped.
I'd tell my mates it's a **gadget** for people who want to look clever.
think: I think nothing much changes for me, and **small-client tax** must be right every time.
I do worry the bigger **chains** could slowly pinch our customers.
do: Keep doing the returns by **hand** and finish my ACA exams.
Look at buying a small **flat** with my girlfriend Tia in two years.
feel: I feel **settled**, with a small knot about the bigger chains.
S0.quote: I'd rather do a return properly than check what a chatbot did, because I'm the one signing it off.
fieldNote: Gareth is **secure** now, but names a slow worry about bigger rivals.
His distrust of tools comes from **accuracy**, not fear.
He plans a **flat** with his girlfriend, so stability matters.

steps.text: Keep doing the tax returns by hand and finish ACA exams
Look at a flat to buy with my girlfriend Tia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, but nobody should rush. At work I'd tell Mr Bell we should watch what the bigger firms do before we spend money. I'd say it down the pub too, but not much, because people get tired of hearing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it hits the typing and the chasing. Most of my day is putting receipt figures into the software and chasing clients, and those are the bits a tool can do. I'd say a third of the work I do now could be done by one person with the right tool. That'd shrink the juniors, and I'm one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Bell to put me with the older clients, the complicated ones, because they won't go to a machine. I'd finally sit down with the practice software's new tool, with Tia helping, since she works in HR and is quick with these things. And I'd put more away, say £700 a month, while pay is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tight in the chest. I'm not panicking, but I didn't think I'd be thinking about this at twenty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would software take first at Okoro & Bell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The simple returns, the ones I do now, the ones that are mostly numbers. Mr Bell would keep the tax planning and the clients who are on first-name terms. That leaves me doing a job I wasn't hired for, or no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mr Bell do if his costs were hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Bell would cut a junior before he cut himself, I think. He'd do it kindly, and he'd say it's about the practice's survival. He isn't a bad boss, but when money's tight, the newest person goes. I'd see it coming and move before it happens.

say: I'd say the change is real, but nobody should **rush**.
I'd tell Mr Bell we should watch what bigger firms do **first**.
think: Privately, a third of my **typing and chasing** work could be done by one person with a tool.
That would shrink the **juniors**, and I am one.
do: Ask Mr Bell to give me the older, **complicated clients**.
Finally try the practice's new **tool**, with Tia helping.
Save **£700** a month while pay is good.
feel: I feel **tight** in the chest, since I didn't expect to think about this at twenty-two.
S1.quote: Mr Bell would cut a junior before he cut himself, I think.
fieldNote: Gareth's **resistance** softens when he sees his own tasks named.
His boss is **pragmatic**, so he expects juniors to go first.
He plans to **move** before it happens, which fits his careful style.

steps.text: Ask Mr Bell for the older, complicated clients
Try the practice's new tool with Tia helping
Save £700 a month while pay is good
Update my CV and talk to a recruiter in Birmingham

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the people running it should be made to slow down. I'd say that to Mr Bell, the lads and anyone who'd listen. And I'd write to my MP, which I wouldn't normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private view: it's the end of my profession as I know it. Tax rules are written down and tax returns are numbers, which is the thing AGI does best. By 2028 I'd be twenty-four with nothing a client will pay a person for. The robots three years after don't matter to me, since I don't work with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the exams, because there's no point paying for a qualification that finishes in the middle of this. I'd keep working and save £900 a month. Then I'd talk to my dad, a bus driver, about whether there's a job in anything that still needs a person at the wheel. I'd also ask Tia whether we should still buy the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. It would be hard to sleep and I'd lose my appetite. I'd go quiet with the lads and feel like I'm carrying a secret.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month if you believed it was only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in charge of the AI firms, mostly. They're making the money and everyone else gets told to adapt. I'd also blame governments for sitting around. I'd be angry at a system, not at one person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep renting, I think, and hold the flat idea until the dust settles. If I buy and lose my income, I'm stuck. I'd rather hold the savings and wait to see, even if that feels like standing still.

say: I'd say it's too **fast**, and the firms behind it should be made to slow down.
I'd write to my **MP**, which I wouldn't normally do.
think: Privately, it's the **end** of my profession as I know it.
Tax rules and returns are **numbers**, which is what AGI does best.
do: Stop the **ACA exams** because they would finish in the middle of this.
Hold off buying a **flat** with Tia.
feel: I feel **frightened**, can't sleep and feel like I'm carrying a secret.
S2.quote: I'd be angry at a system, not at one person.
fieldNote: Gareth sees tax work as **pure numbers**, so he expects it to go quickly.
His anger is **structural**: AI firms and slow governments.
He **freezes** big purchases, which fits his resistant, careful style.

steps.text: Stop paying for the ACA exams
Save £900 a month while the job lasts
Ask my dad about bus driver and transport jobs
Hold off on buying the flat with Tia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be sensible. I'd tell Mr Bell we should talk about what the practice becomes. And I'd write to my MP about retraining money for accountants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same problem but slower. I'd be twenty-seven and should have a professional qualification by then, so I might get a few good years as a manager of the small clients. But I don't trust that, because the clients would go to cheaper services too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the ACA exams in about three years, because a qualified accountant still has some protection. I'd learn the tools bit by bit, starting with the practice software's new helper. I'd also look at a field that needs a licence and a face, like insolvency work or advice for small businesses. And I'd save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit calmer. There's room to move and I can use my usual slow style, which works better here than in the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you more room. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, but a cheaper one and further out. A flat is somewhere to live whatever happens, and I'd keep enough in the bank to cover a year of payments. That's the safe version of the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Mr Bell about moving the practice towards advice and tax planning, because that's where people sit across a desk. He'd probably listen, he's practical. I'd also learn how clients feel about it, because I'd be the one on the phone.

say: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be **sensible** and plan.
I'd write to my MP about **retraining money** for accountants.
think: It's the same problem, only **slower**, and clients would go to cheaper services too.
I might get a few good years as **manager** of the small clients.
do: Finish the **ACA exams** in about three years.
Learn the tools **bit by bit**, starting with the practice helper.
Look at **licensed advice work** for small businesses.
feel: I feel a bit **calmer**, with room to move at my slow pace.
S3.quote: A flat is somewhere to live whatever happens, and I'd keep enough in the bank to cover a year of payments.
fieldNote: Gareth's **slow style** suits five years better than two.
He wants a **licensed**, face-to-face niche for protection.
Buying the flat now means **stability**, not speculation.

steps.text: Finish the ACA exams within three years
Learn the practice's helper tool bit by bit
Buy a cheaper flat further out with Tia
Write to my MP about retraining money for accountants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a long way off, and I'm not going to lose sleep. I'd say we should still prepare, with training and fair rules. And I'd say it quietly, because I don't like drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years is enough to plan around. By 2036 I'd be thirty-two, hopefully qualified and maybe running a small practice branch. The tools will have changed things a lot, but I'd have had time to learn them, even slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and the exams, and save for the flat. I'd learn one tool a year, which is about my speed. I'd also start a small advice service for sole traders at weekends, since that's something that grows from my own clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. It feels like the sort of thing I can handle at my own speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you keep doing the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep talking to people in person, because that's what I'm good at. I'd keep my own pace with the tools and I'd keep a good cushion. I'd also keep asking Mr Bell hard questions about where the practice is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone younger than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine to be a bit slow, but don't be proud about it. Learn a bit every year, and keep a cushion. I'd tell them my mistake was assuming the tools were hype for too long.

say: I'd say it's a long way off, but we should still **prepare**.
I'd keep it **quiet**, because I don't like drama.
think: Ten years is enough to **plan around**, even at my slow speed.
By 2036 I'd be thirty-two, hopefully **qualified** and running part of a practice.
do: Keep the job and the **exams**, and save for the flat.
Learn **one tool a year**, which is about my speed.
Start a weekend **advice service** for sole traders.
feel: I feel **fine**, like something I can handle at my own speed.
S4.quote: I'd say it's fine to be a bit slow, but don't be proud about it.
fieldNote: Gareth's **pragmatism** shows: slow learning is fine if it is steady.
He admits to **assuming** the tools were hype for too long.
A weekend service is his first **side income** idea across the five.

steps.text: Finish the exams and keep the Okoro & Bell job
Learn one new tool every year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I'm slow with new things, and two years gives me no time to catch up, or to find a role that still needs a person. What would help is the government being straight about what's coming, paid retraining, and firms like Mr Bell's getting support to keep their juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say I was wrong to dismiss it. I thought it was hype, and I think a lot of people my age are the same. It's easier to say it's overblown than to admit you might have to change.

headlineQuote: I thought it was hype, and I think a lot of people my age are the same.
portrait: Gareth, 22, is a **junior accountant** at a nine-person tax practice in Birmingham, and never uses AI tools.
He is pragmatic, slow with new software, and saves hard with **no debt** thanks to his parents.
His own tasks, typing and chasing receipts, are the ones he expects to go, which turns doubt into **anxiety**.
He blames **systems**, meaning AI firms and slow governments, more than any person.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because he is slow with new things and would have no time to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: Governments being **straight** about what's coming, plus paid retraining.
Support for small firms like Mr Bell's to **keep** their juniors.
